name: Triangle Innovation Point West, Chatham County
heading: 3. Triangle Innovation Point West, Chatham County — 750 MW Proposed
brief: ECO TIP West LLC is pursuing a 750 MW data center at Triangle Innovation Point West, a more than 400-acre heavy-industrial property near Moncure in southeastern Chatham County. The developer says it had spent more than $11 million pursuing the campus before county commissioners imposed a temporary data-center moratorium in February 2026. Its stated figure is a future electrical requirement, not a utility meter reading or proof of a fully approved 750 MW electrical connection. The project acquired a clearer legal path on September 17, 2026 , when Superior Court Judge John Morris granted summary judgment in favor of ECO TIP West. The Chatham Journal’s examination of the ruling says the judgment establishes liability and attorney-fee entitlement in the developer’s challenge to the moratorium; damages remained for later proceedings. The decision allows the developer’s project to advance despite the pause, but does not itself supply construction permits, financing, an electric-service agreement or a final tenant . Chatham County was reviewing its options. The dispute dates to Chatham Coun

name: Natelli Holdings, Vance County
heading: 2. Natelli Holdings, Vance County — 900 MW Proposed
brief: Natelli Holdings submitted a multi-phase plan for a 900 MW data center campus on approximately 529 acres near U.S. Highway 158 and Poplar Creek Road outside Henderson. The September 9 filing, compiled from county documents , describes up to 12 data center buildings totaling approximately 4 million square feet over four phases. Developer Tom Natelli has said his team completed substantial planning and has discussed grid service with Duke Energy. This is still a proposed project, not 900 MW of operating servers. The developer’s application arrived as county officials considered new requirements for buffering, cooling, noise, generators and utility service. On September 14 , the Vance County Board of Commissioners adopted a 60-day moratorium by a 5–2 vote , according to WIZS News . The pause is scheduled to terminate November 13 or earlier if the county adopts replacement standards. Whether Natelli’s filed application qualifies for protection under pre-existing rules or the moratorium’s exemptions is a legal and administrative question; the filing should not be labeled final approval. name: Amazon Web Services, Richmond County
heading: 1. Amazon Web Services, Richmond County — Approximately 1,000 MW Reported Demand
brief: Amazon Web Services is constructing a $10 billion cloud and AI campus at the Energy Way Industrial Park near Hamlet in Richmond County. North Carolina announced the project in June 2025 , alongside a pledge of at least 500 permanent jobs . Amazon broke ground in October 2025, and public permit filings describe a large phased campus with approximately 20 to 21 buildings planned across several years. This is the most advanced new megascale data center development in the ranking. The project’s roughly 1 GW power requirement comes from WUNC’s September 16 reporting rather than a detailed public Amazon IT-load specification. That number is best read as an estimate of eventual facility electricity demand, including non-IT systems, not as proof that 1,000 MW of computing racks have been installed or energized. One of the most consequential issues is how the site will receive power before permanent connections are ready. name: Critical Data House Project Fighting Pike, Williston
heading: 3. Critical Data House Project Fighting Pike, Williston — 455 MW Planned, Delayed
brief: Critical Data House’s Project Fighting Pike is a proposed seven-building, 455 MW campus on approximately 300 acres near U.S. Highway 2 and 56th Street NW in Williston. The published development plan groups the buildings into three phases and includes utility areas, roads, stormwater ponds and security access. The developer has discussed up to $5 billion for construction and another $5 billion for computing equipment , figures that depend on the project actually proceeding. Williston commissioners approved important planning steps in March 2025 , as KFYR reported at the time . That approval established a route through land-use review; it did not construct data halls, secure a hyperscale tenant or switch on 455 MW of servers. The project has been described as primarily intended for cloud and AI customers rather than a new cryptocurrency mining operation, but no binding end-user contract was verified in the public materials reviewed. name: Geronimo Power Harmony Energy Park, Cass County
heading: 2. Geronimo Power Harmony Energy Park, Cass County — 540 MW Proposed
brief: Geronimo Power submitted a conditional-use permit application on September 15, 2026 , for a data center on a 640-acre section of Harmony Township northeast of Casselton and north of Mapleton. Its proposal includes two main data center buildings , roads and related infrastructure. The developer says the initial utility service could reach 540 MW and that roughly 160 acres would contain buildings and improved surfaces, with more than three-quarters of the section remaining open land. As of October 29, the data center had not received its local conditional-use approval . Harmony Township had considered a possible 24-month moratorium affecting large energy and computing projects, but a scheduled October 22 vote was canceled. The developer has sought discussion with residents and offered to pause consideration of its application for six months. Neither a suspended hearing nor a conditional-use filing establishes a completed service agreement, a named hyperscale tenant or physical data center construction. name: Atlas Power Data Center, Williston Area
heading: 1. Atlas Power Data Center, Williston Area — 700 MW Phased Development Plan
brief: Atlas Power’s existing computing complex west of Williston is the largest phased power ambition in this comparison. In a January 26, 2022 announcement , North Dakota’s governor described a $1.9 billion development on roughly 77 acres built by FX Solutions and served by Mountrail-Williams Electric Cooperative. The original schedule called for 240 MW in the first phase , a rise to 500 MW in the second, and an eventual 700 MW in the third. The project was designed chiefly for Bitcoin mining and other high-performance computing workloads. Atlas has operated at the Williston-area site since 2023. A 2026 statewide data center roundup described the facility as operating at 700 MW, but an independently verified utility-meter record proving 700 MW currently energized was not available in the sources reviewed. This article therefore treats 700 MW as the announced ultimate buildout , not established real-time draw. name: Cologix Johnstown Campus
heading: 3. Cologix Johnstown Campus — 800 MW Planned Full Buildout
brief: Cologix announced a new hyperscale and AI-ready campus in Johnstown, Licking County , after acquiring approximately 154 acres in November 2024. Its original company announcement describes a potential 800 MW across eight data center buildings and approximately 2 million square feet , with more than $7 billion in anticipated development spending. The 800 MW figure is a full-build opportunity, not evidence that eight buildings or all their substations are commissioned. The project has since gained more concrete shape. A June 1, 2026 regional announcement describes Cologix’s initial investments in Johnstown and nearby Orange Township as more than $1.1 billion combined, with at least 90 expected direct jobs across those two developments. These are separate sites , and the Orange Township investment cannot be treated as another 800 MW added to the Johnstown master plan. Cologix’s own COL8 facility page identifies the site at 11719 Duncan Plains Road and describes high-density, liquid-cooling-ready space with fiber access to its broader Columbus network. name: Meta Prometheus, New Albany
heading: 2. Meta Prometheus, New Albany — Gigawatt-Scale AI Supercluster, First Phase Operating
brief: Meta’s Prometheus facility in New Albany is substantially further along. In an October 19 engineering report , Meta said the first phase is complete and has already been used to train its Muse models. The company describes the installation as a gigawatt-scale AI supercluster , which is the basis for ranking its planned scale ahead of the 800 MW Johnstown development. It does not report a precisely metered 1,000 MW IT load currently operating. Meta says the cluster includes hundreds of thousands of GPUs across conventional data halls and rapidly deployed computing structures connected through high-speed fiber networks. It expects the system to grow toward approximately one million GPUs at full scale. Its announced equipment includes NVIDIA GB200 and GB300 platforms, with newer systems planned. These are hardware deployment descriptions from the operator, not independent measurements of total computing power. Independent data center researcher Epoch AI estimates that Prometheus had approximately 471 MW of IT power in operation in its October 2026 model, with a projection exceeding 1 GW

name: PORTS-Pike Technology Campus, Piketon
heading: 1. PORTS-Pike Technology Campus, Piketon — 8 GW Planned IT Capacity
brief: The largest documented Ohio data center development is PORTS-Pike , the proposed AI campus at the former Portsmouth Gaseous Diffusion Plant near Piketon. In its August 17 announcement , OpenAI said it agreed to secure approximately 8 gigawatts of critical IT capacity from developer SB Energy . NVIDIA’s disclosed arrangement provides credit support for an initial 4.25 GW of land, power and building capacity, plus an option on the remaining 3.75 GW. SB Energy is to own and operate the development under a 20-year arrangement with OpenAI as the customer. The project’s broader 10 GW number has also appeared in federal and county presentations. It describes the proposed whole-site power and infrastructure envelope, while OpenAI’s 8 GW IT figure refers to computing equipment power. Separately, the Department of Energy described plans for 10 GW of new generation , including 9.2 GW of natural gas , supported by new transmission. name: Cloverleaf Project Open Sky, Piedmont
heading: 3. Cloverleaf Project Open Sky, Piedmont — About 1,400 MW Proposed
brief: Cloverleaf Infrastructure is pursuing a large campus on the north side of Piedmont in Canadian County. The company’s filing for its initial approximately 633-acre development describes six data center buildings , each approximately 352,800 square feet , along with a substation, warehouses, internal roads, landscaping and drainage facilities. An expanded footprint, including land options in nearby Kingfisher County, supports a long-range aim of around 1.4 GW of electricity demand . The first six-building development is expected to need about 600 MW ; 1.4 GW is not a commissioned first phase. The project has seen extensive public review. On October 22, 2026 , Piedmont’s City Council voted 4–1 to endorse an amended master design plan that keeps Frisco Road open, while separate annexation, rezoning and site approvals still remained. According to a chronology of council proceedings , the developer had previously revised its proposals several times amid local concerns. name: Core Scientific Muskogee
heading: 2. Core Scientific Muskogee — 1,500 MW Planned Gross Power; Existing Capacity Secured
brief: Core Scientific has a materially different position in Muskogee: it owns or controls operational infrastructure and is constructing more high-density colocation space for AI customers. On August 14 , the company announced the completion of its approximately $444 million acquisition of Polaris DS , securing access to around 440 MW of existing gross, grid-connected power capacity under agreements with Oklahoma Gas & Electric. That electricity supply was already being used at the Polaris site, principally for Bitcoin mining. With Polaris and adjacent development land, Core Scientific plans to expand the Muskogee complex toward 1,500 MW of gross power , or approximately 1,000 MW of future leasable data center power . Those company targets include new electrical infrastructure and potential behind-the-meter generation that remain to be built or contracted. The existing 440 MW is part of the expansion strategy, not an extra amount to add to the 1,500 MW headline . name: Project Thunderbird, Enid
heading: 1. Project Thunderbird, Enid — Up to 2,750 MW of Planned IT Capacity
brief: Project Thunderbird is the largest announced Oklahoma development by its developer’s stated 2.75 GW of eventual critical IT capacity . Plainsmen Holdings, a group led by Enid business owners, proposes a four-campus data center corridor and related utility infrastructure covering approximately 1,735 acres at full buildout. Its model also envisions up to 3.3 GW of dedicated power generation . The 3.3 GW is a separate supply-side design envelope, not another 3.3 GW of server demand to add to the 2.75 GW. A significant land-use decision arrived this week. On October 27, 2026 , Enid’s mayor and City Commission voted 6–1 to approve the developer’s three rezoning requests affecting its North and West campus areas. Plainsmen’s October 28 update confirms that the planned South campus still needs annexation and rezoning, while the East campus involves a separate land option with the city. name: STACK Infrastructure POR03, Hillsboro
heading: 3. STACK Infrastructure POR03, Hillsboro — Approximately 200 MW Total Critical Capacity
brief: STACK Infrastructure operates and markets its POR03 campus in Hillsboro as a six-building development on approximately 55 acres with 200 MW of total critical capacity . Crucially, STACK separately identifies about 72 MW of operational critical capacity , 25 MW of near-term availability and 96 MW of expansion capacity . Those descriptions distinguish already operating data halls from space that still depends on construction, fit-out and customer requirements. STACK’s rounded campus headline is not a reading from an electricity meter. The company’s site breakdown lists three existing 24 MW facilities—POR03A, POR03B and POR03C—followed by a 25 MW POR03D building and a planned combined 96 MW POR03E/F development. These are differentiated phases within one identified campus, not separate 200 MW projects that can be added together. The site is designed for dense cloud, machine-learning and AI workloads with high-capacity networking, redundant electrical equipment and low-water-use cooling strategies. name: Rowan Percheron, Boardman
heading: 2. Rowan Percheron, Boardman — 300 MW Planned Campus
brief: Rowan Digital Infrastructure describes Percheron as a 300 MW hyperscale campus across about 275 acres in the Columbia River Gorge near Boardman. Rowan began site due diligence in late 2022, secured rezoning approvals in 2023, and closed its land acquisition in 2024. The developer lists a phased buildout targeting completion by 2030 . That is a future delivery target, not evidence of 300 MW of energized servers in October 2026. Percheron represents a different development strategy from an operating colocation building: its owner secures industrial land, develops a utility and permitting pathway, prepares the campus for major cloud customers and then advances construction in stages. Rowan says its property is close to established fiber corridors and power infrastructure. Company marketing has not established a full 300 MW of signed customer IT load, commissioned substations or an independently verified delivery schedule for each phase. name: Amazon Threemile/Boardman
heading: 1. Amazon Threemile/Boardman — Hypothetical 1,000 MW Campus Envelope
brief: Amazon Web Services acquired roughly 1,300 acres near Boardman in Morrow County for a potential data center development that has drawn attention under the Threemile or exascale label. Earlier planning documents presented a hypothetical 1,000 MW complex with up to 20 buildings and approximately 4 million square feet . The figure gives a sense of the maximum footprint explored in site planning. It is not a confirmed Amazon construction order, an energized grid connection or the official capacity of a funded 20-building phase. Amazon explicitly narrowed that interpretation in a September 14 interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting . Roger Wehner, its vice president for economic development, told host Dave Miller that the current vision is more like the company’s four-building campus model , potentially repeated incrementally as demand and local needs allow. When asked whether Amazon planned the full 1 GW scale, he said the company’s current vision was not to develop at that scale . name: Aligned Project Phoenix, Shippingport
heading: 3. Aligned Project Phoenix, Shippingport — 2 GW Planned Campus, Construction Started
brief: Aligned Data Centers broke ground on Project Phoenix on September 10, 2026 , at a former industrial power property near the decommissioned Bruce Mansfield coal plant in Shippingport, Beaver County . The company describes a 2 GW, three-facility campus on a site along the Ohio River, with approximately 2 million square feet of planned data center space . The groundbreaking marks a construction milestone, not the commissioning of 2 GW of servers. Aligned projects approximately $10 billion in regional economic investment , about 3,000 construction jobs and roughly 640 long-term operating positions . These figures are developer forecasts, not completed spending or a verified head count. Its plans include dedicated energy infrastructure and commitments intended to reduce the potential impact of project-related grid upgrades on other utility customers. name: TECfusions Keystone Connect, Upper Burrell
heading: 2. TECfusions Keystone Connect, Upper Burrell — 3 GW IT Ambition, Small Initial Phase Operating
brief: TECfusions Keystone Connect , built around the former Alcoa research complex in Upper Burrell Township, Westmoreland County , has the largest explicit IT-power development target among the three entries. The company markets approximately 1,395 to 1,400 acres for an eventual 3 GW of IT load , using former research buildings as the foundation for a much larger AI computing campus. Its Keystone Connect project sheet describes 3 GW as the site’s total capability, not capacity already operating. The more precise status appears in the company’s 2026 investor materials . TECfusions identifies approximately 2 MW of live computing in its initial building, with 10 MW more contracted for buildout . It describes the remaining 3 GW as a phased, five-year pipeline to 2031 . That creates a dramatic difference between operating megawatts and the project’s promoted long-range potential. The latter depends on additional construction, electricity supply, customer demand and financing. The conversion has faced local challenges. name: Homer City Energy Campus, Indiana County
heading: 1. Homer City Energy Campus, Indiana County — 4.4–4.5 GW Planned Power Generation
brief: The largest overall electrical development tied to a Pennsylvania data center campus is Homer City Energy Campus , a more than 3,200-acre redevelopment of the former Homer City coal-fired generating station. Developer Homer City Redevelopment and construction contractor Kiewit plan a large new natural-gas power system, with seven GE Vernova gas turbines intended to supply future AI and high-performance computing facilities as well as the wider grid. The project was announced in April 2025 with up to 4.5 GW of generating capacity ; subsequent air-permit and engineering descriptions use around 4.4 GW . These numbers describe intended gas-fired electricity production, not 4.5 GW of computers or guaranteed IT load . Developer material says some of the electricity could be exported to the grid. The future data center’s own load, tenants and construction schedule require separate evidence. Physical work on the power-campus redevelopment is substantial. name: Lumen Providence
heading: 3. Lumen Providence — 0.6 MW Listed, Operating
brief: Lumen’s Providence facility is part of the traditional carrier and network-colocation market that developed around downtown Providence. Data Center Map places its Providence 1 site at 375 Promenade Street . Research directories list it as operating and associate roughly 10,400 square feet of total building area with the site. The facility helps regional businesses connect computing equipment to telecom infrastructure rather than functioning as a hyperscale AI training campus. The Baxtel Rhode Island market directory associates 0.6 MW of capacity with Lumen Technologies’ one operating state facility . Since this is a provider-level directory figure and no matching recent Lumen technical specification was established, it should be treated as a reported reference point, not a confirmed current IT load . The public record does not disclose how much of the rated capacity is occupied by paying customers. Lumen’s comparatively modest published scale highlights a different kind of data center economy. name: Crown Castle Providence, 300 Carpenter Street
heading: 2. Crown Castle Providence, 300 Carpenter Street — Approximately 1 MW Reported
brief: The operating colocation and network facility at 300 Carpenter Street is associated with former owner Crown Castle Fiber , whose fiber business was sold to a Zayo buyer in 2026. The facility’s source-linked project record identifies it as an active Providence site and notes the ownership transition, but does not confirm a new site-specific operating contract or publish a current electrical rating. A separate commercial facility tracker reports approximately 1 MW and 12,023 square feet of building area . This is a secondary dataset estimate. It is not a company-authored assertion that one megawatt of servers is running today, nor does it establish that every square foot is dedicated to computing racks. Those limits matter because other industry records for this address explicitly say electrical capacity is not publicly reported. Carpenter Street is an established part of Providence’s fiber and network infrastructure rather than a new land-intensive AI development. name: Prov.net PVD2, 304 Carpenter Street
heading: 1. Prov.net PVD2, 304 Carpenter Street — 1 MW Critical Power
brief: The best-documented operating capacity among the three belongs to Prov.net’s PVD2 facility at 304 Carpenter Street . In an October 18, 2021 announcement , global network provider Hurricane Electric described the facility as offering up to 15,000 square feet, 1 MW of critical power and 200 tons of N+1 cooling . The power rating describes designed critical-service capacity, not verified continuous consumption . Its site address and network presence remain listed by Hurricane Electric’s own point-of-presence directory . Hurricane Electric’s arrival provided access to its international IP backbone through 100-gigabit, 10-gigabit and one-gigabit Ethernet connections. Those network links can support regional companies that need reliable connections, redundancy and low-latency access to services beyond Rhode Island. The site was described as part of Providence’s dense fiber corridor, a characteristic that can be more valuable to a local carrier hotel than a very large parcel of inexpensive land. name: QTS York County
heading: 3. QTS York County — About 300 MW Reported, Under Construction
brief: In the Rock Hill area, QTS is developing a nine-building campus in three phases. The company says its approved project represents approximately $8 billion in planned investment . Four buildings make up its initial phase, while the other five would follow as development proceeds. QTS says two buildings are under construction and none is yet operating; more work is expected as the first phase advances. A facility-level project record reports roughly 300 MW of planned power, but QTS’s current public community page does not give a comparable total megawatt figure. Treat 300 MW as an industry-reported campus figure, not measured server consumption or a confirmed utility delivery schedule. QTS says its air-cooled design uses ambient air as the final heat sink, and forecasts substantial construction employment and long-term technical work. WCNC’s February 11, 2026 report covers QTS’s York County project, local questions and construction activity.

name: NorthMark Valara, Spartanburg
heading: 2. NorthMark Valara, Spartanburg — 457 MW Planned, Construction Underway
brief: The Valara High Performance Compute Center is being built at the former Kohler manufacturing site on South Pine Street in Spartanburg. A development agreement considered by Spartanburg County describes a 457 MW data center project over approximately 294 acres, with at least $2.76 billion in proposed investment. Its model centers on substantial on-site power generation rather than treating the entire demand as a simple purchase from an existing local substation. On September 18, South Carolina’s Department of Environmental Services approved a construction air permit for 11 simple-cycle combustion turbines . That is an air-permit decision, not a blanket finding that every construction, land-use or operating approval has been resolved. On October 22, County Council gave first reading to a revised development agreement ; final approval still requires additional proceedings. The project has drawn organized objections about air emissions, noise, local oversight and water demand. name: Savannah River Site AI Campus
heading: 1. Savannah River Site AI Campus — 1,000 MW Proposed, Lease Not Final
brief: The largest announced data center project on this list is an approximately 1 GW AI campus at the federal Savannah River Site . On July 20, the Department of Energy’s National Nuclear Security Administration selected Amentum for negotiations over a phased lease. DC BLOX has identified itself as the consortium’s digital-infrastructure partner. The federal concept pairs that 1 GW of data center capacity with approximately 2 GW of dedicated generation , starting with natural gas and describing a possible transition toward nuclear technology. Those numbers represent different things: the 2 GW is proposed generating capacity, not a 2 GW server load. The planned campus is not yet online, and neither a final lease nor completion of the required permits and security reviews was established in the July announcement. The federal location could give developers access to a large industrial setting, existing technical expertise and the opportunity to coordinate energy and compute investment.
